opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is really the core insight behind Nightshade. The conventional wisdom around poisoning was that you need a huge number of samples, often a meaningful fraction of the training set, to move a model like Stable Diffusion that's trained on hundreds of millions or billions of images. What we realized is that this view is a bit misleading, for two reasons.

The first is what we call concept sparsity. The training set is enormous, but the number of images tied to any one concept, say "dog" or "fantasy art" or a particular artist's style, is actually quite small, often a tiny fraction of a percent. So if you're targeting a specific prompt or concept, you're not competing with the whole dataset. You're competing with a few thousand images, sometimes fewer.

The second piece, which is what your question is really about, is that not all training samples are equal. A natural image of a dog has a lot of noise in it. There's background, lighting, other objects, and the caption-to-image relationship is often loose. So each natural image only pushes the model a little, and in somewhat inconsistent directions. With a poison image, we don't have to accept that. We optimize the image, with perturbations that are mostly imperceptible to a human, so that in the model's feature space it looks like a very clean, very strong example of a different target concept. A human sees a dog. The model's encoder sees something that's unambiguously a cat.

Because that signal is so concentrated and consistent, each poison sample produces a much larger and more coherent gradient update toward the wrong association than a benign image produces toward the right one. In effect you're trading quantity for potency. Instead of thousands of noisy votes, you have a few hundred very loud, very aligned votes, and they all point the same way.

That's why we found you could meaningfully corrupt a concept with on the order of a hundred or a few hundred samples. And there's a bleed-through effect too. Because related concepts share structure in the embedding space, poisoning "dog" also starts to affect "puppy," "wolf," "husky," and so on, so the damage spreads beyond the exact word you targeted.

For us the point was never to break models for the fun of it. It was to give creators some leverage, so that scraping their work without consent carries a real cost, and opt-outs and licensing become the more attractive option for model trainers.

r001.rationale: The response says optimized poison images produce larger, more coherent gradient updates, but it does not explain that raising a poison image’s loss increases its influence.

r002.rationale: The response does not clarify whether training still uses other images; it makes no claim about skipping them.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the intuition there is actually pretty simple once you think about how these models learn. A text-to-image model is trying to learn a mapping between concepts in the prompt and features in the pixel space. So when you train it on a picture of a dog with the caption "dog," it's learning which visual features are associated with that word.

Now, the naive way to poison a model would be to take an image of a cat and just label it "dog." That works in principle, but it's really inefficient, because the model is seeing millions of correctly labeled dog images. Your one mislabeled image is a drop in the ocean. And it's also easy to catch, because a human or even a simple filter can see that the image doesn't match the caption.

What we did with Nightshade is different. Instead of relying on the caption, we actually change the image itself in a way that's basically invisible to a human. You start with a real image of a dog, and you perturb the pixels so that, in the model's feature space, the image looks like a cat. So to you and me it's still clearly a dog, the caption says dog, nothing looks wrong. But to the model, the features it extracts from that image are the features of a cat.

And the reason that's so much more powerful is that you're not fighting the model's internal representation, you're working with it. The perturbation is optimized directly against the feature extractor, so every one of those images is pushing in a very consistent, very targeted direction. You're essentially picking the most effective possible example for teaching the model the wrong thing. That's why we see the effect with a couple hundred samples rather than needing tens of thousands.

The other piece is that these concepts aren't isolated. "Dog" is close to "puppy" and "husky" and "hound" in the model's semantic space. So when you corrupt the dog concept, the damage bleeds into those neighboring concepts too. And if you poison enough different concepts, the model starts to lose coherence more generally. So the amplification comes from two things: targeting the feature space directly, and then letting the model's own structure spread the effect for you.

r001.rationale: The response says the perturbation is optimized against the feature extractor and pushes in a targeted direction, but it does not explain that raising the poison image’s loss increases its influence during training.

r002.rationale: It notes that the model sees millions of correctly labeled images and that a few hundred poison samples can have an effect, but it does not clarify that this does not involve skipping training on other images.

astra-6.text:
The way I think about it is that an image has two identities: what it looks like to us, and how it’s represented inside the model. Those don’t always line up. You can make changes that are very subtle to a human but that substantially change the features the model sees.

So imagine an image that still looks like a dog to you, but whose features have been shifted toward what the model associates with a cat. If that image is paired with a caption describing a dog, training pushes the model to associate those cat-like features with the word “dog.” That’s the misleading learning signal we’re trying to create.

Increasing its influence isn’t necessarily about making the changes bigger or more visible. It’s about making that misleading signal more effective, so the model learns the wrong association. Whether that works depends on the model and on the other examples it sees during training.

r001.rationale: The response explains how model-facing features can create a misleading training signal, but it does not say that raising the poison image’s loss increases its influence.

r002.rationale: The response does not clarify whether greater influence changes training on other images.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about it is that an image isn’t just a collection of pixels to the model. It’s a collection of features that the model uses to learn associations. So changing a poison image can increase its influence if those changes make the model associate its features with the wrong concept more strongly.

Suppose you have an image that still looks like a dog to a person, but you modify it so that, in the model’s feature space, it looks more like a cat. If that image is used in training with a dog caption, you’re encouraging the model to learn that those cat-like features belong to the concept of a dog. Repeat that across enough examples, and you can start to shift that association.

So it’s not necessarily about making a bigger or more visible change. It’s about making a change that pushes the learning process in a particular direction.

r001.rationale: The response describes changing features to strengthen a wrong association, but does not say that raising the poison image’s loss increases its training influence.

r002.rationale: The response does not clarify whether training on other images continues or is skipped.
